note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/03 Chemical bonding/3.7 Dot-and-cross diagrams.md
outline: Use dots and crosses to distinguish the valence electrons originally supplied by each atom. Ionic diagrams show electron transfer and separate bracketed ions with charges; covalent diagrams show shared pairs and lone pairs. In coordinate bonding, both electrons in a shared pair come from one donor atom. Count all valence electrons, adjusting for ionic charge, then verify bonding pairs, lone pairs and formal charges. Include electron-deficient BF₃, expanded-octet PCl₅ and odd-electron NO where relevant.

misconceptions.statement: Ionic compounds are drawn as shared electron pairs between atoms.
misconceptions.refutation: An ionic diagram shows separate bracketed ions with charges after electron transfer.
misconceptions.contrast: In MgO, Mg is [Mg]²⁺ and O is [O]²⁻ with a complete outer shell.

misconceptions.statement: Every bond in CO is an ordinary shared pair, or the coordinate pair goes from carbon to oxygen.
misconceptions.refutation: In the dot-and-cross convention for CO, oxygen donates a pair to carbon.
misconceptions.contrast: Show two ordinary shared pairs and one O→C coordinate pair.

misconceptions.statement: Atoms in dot-and-cross diagrams must always obey the octet rule.
misconceptions.refutation: The syllabus includes electron-deficient, expanded-octet and odd-electron species.
misconceptions.contrast: BF₃ has six electrons around B; PCl₅ has ten around P; NO has an unpaired electron.

misconceptions.statement: A coordinate bond contains one electron from each bonded atom.
misconceptions.refutation: The donor supplies both electrons of the shared pair; the acceptor supplies an empty orbital.
misconceptions.contrast: In NH₄⁺, N of NH₃ supplies both electrons to H⁺.

worked.problem: Demonstrate a dot-and-cross diagram for $\ce{NH4+}$ formed from $\ce{NH3}$ and $\ce{H+}$.

steps.do: Count five N valence electrons, one from each of four H atoms and subtract one for the positive charge: eight electrons.
steps.why: The charge changes the total valence-electron count.

steps.do: Draw four N–H shared pairs inside brackets marked +; use a distinct symbol for the N lone pair donated to H⁺.
steps.why: The fourth bond is coordinate on formation: both electrons originate from N.

steps.do: Check four bonding pairs, no lone pair, eight electrons around N and only two around each H.
steps.why: The count detects missing or duplicated electrons.

faded.problem: Draw $\ce{H3O+}$ from $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{H+}$; how many bonding pairs surround O?

items.stem: Show the outer-shell electrons by drawing dot-and-cross diagrams for (a) MgO, (b) NH3 and (c) NH4+ formed when NH3 donates a lone pair to H+. For (a), use dots for electrons originally from O and crosses for electrons originally from Mg; omit inner shells and show no electrons on Mg2+. For (b) and (c), use dots for electrons originally from N and crosses for electrons originally from H. Include all lone pairs and any required brackets and charges.

scheme.point: (a) Separate bracketed Mg and O ions with charges 2+ and 2− respectively; no shared pair between the ions.
(a) Eight electrons around O: six dots originally from O and two crosses transferred from Mg; omit inner shells and show no electrons on Mg.
(b) Three N–H shared pairs, each containing one dot from N and one cross from H.
(b) One lone pair of two dots on N, no further electrons and no ionic charge.
(c) Four N–H shared pairs: three dot–cross pairs and one dot–dot pair donated by N to the incoming H+; no lone pair remains on N.
(c) Enclose the whole NH4+ ion in brackets with an overall + charge; show no additional electrons.

items.explanation: MgO contains separate Mg2+ and O2− ions after transfer of two electrons from Mg to O. NH3 has three shared N–H pairs and one nitrogen lone pair; donation of that lone pair to H+ forms a fourth shared pair in NH4+, leaving no nitrogen lone pair and an overall + charge. The dot–dot pair records the origin of the coordinate pair; all four N–H bonds are equivalent after formation.
hints: Start by identifying the atoms and the electrons they originally supply.
Distinguish electron transfer from electron sharing, and track the origin of each electron.
Write the neutral-atom valence counts for Mg, O, N and H before arranging the electrons; H+ contributes no electron.

Sketch a complete outer-shell dot-and-cross diagram of $\ce{CO}$ using the conventional coordinate-bond construction. Use dots for electrons originally supplied by C and crosses for those supplied by O. Show every shared and lone pair, and label the donor-to-acceptor direction of the coordinate pair with an arrow. The molecule has no overall charge.

scheme.point: Three shared pairs between C and O: two dot–cross pairs and one cross–cross pair, with no additional bonding electrons.
One dot–dot lone pair on C and one cross–cross lone pair on O; no additional non-bonding electrons (ten electrons in total).
The coordinate pair is labelled $\ce{O -> C}$, with the arrow from oxygen to carbon; the molecule has no overall ionic charge.

items.explanation: Carbon supplies four and oxygen six valence electrons, giving ten in total. Two ordinary dot–cross pairs and one oxygen-supplied cross–cross pair leave one lone pair on each atom and an octet around each. The symbols record electron origin in this conventional construction, so the coordinate arrow points from O to C.
hints: Use the symbols to keep a separate account of the electrons supplied by each atom.
Place the shared electrons first, then check the remaining electrons against each atom’s original contribution.
Write the neutral-atom valence counts from the periodic table before assigning symbols to pairs; a donated pair must use two symbols from the same atom.

items.stem: Sketch a complete dot-and-cross diagram for one formula unit of ionic $\ce{Mg2Si}$. Use dots for electrons originally supplied by Si and crosses for electrons originally supplied by either Mg atom. Show separate ions, all brackets and charges, and every electron from the original outer shells after transfer. Omit inner shells and show no electrons on the magnesium ions.

scheme.point: Two separate $[\ce{Mg}]^{2+}$ ions and one separate $[\ce{Si}]^{4-}$ ion, each enclosed in its own square brackets with its charge.
Eight outer electrons around Si, drawn as four pairs: four dots originally supplied by Si and four crosses transferred from Mg.
Each Mg supplies two of the transferred crosses; no electrons remain drawn on either Mg ion and no shared pairs or covalent bonds join the ions.

items.explanation: Each of the two Mg atoms transfers two outer electrons, so Si gains four electrons and has eight in its outer shell. The diagram contains two $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ ions and one $\ce{Si^{4-}}$ ion, giving a total charge of $2(+2)-4=0$. The dots and crosses on Si distinguish its original electrons from the transferred electrons.
hints: Start from the formula to decide how many atoms of each element must be represented.
Use the group numbers to count the electrons available for transfer, then balance the total charge.
List the original outer-shell electrons separately for each atom before moving any symbols to the ion that gains electrons.

items.stem: Sketch a complete outer-shell dot-and-cross diagram for an isolated $\ce{BF3}$ molecule. Use dots for electrons originally supplied by B and crosses for those supplied by F. Include every shared pair and lone pair, and show any overall charge if needed. Beneath the sketch, state the number of electrons surrounding B and whether it has a complete octet.

scheme.point: Three B–F single bonds, each represented by one dot–cross shared pair.
Each F has three cross–cross lone pairs; no lone pairs or additional electrons are placed on B (24 electrons in the whole diagram).
The molecule is neutral, with no overall ionic charge; six electrons surround B, so B has an incomplete octet.

items.explanation: The total valence-electron count is $3+3(7)=24$: six electrons form three B–F shared pairs and the other eighteen form nine lone pairs on the fluorines. Boron has six surrounding electrons and no lone pair, while each F has an octet. Adding a lone pair to B would invent electrons and incorrectly force a complete octet.
hints: Check whether this central atom is one of the exceptions to the octet rule.
Count all available electrons before distributing bonding pairs and terminal-atom lone pairs.
Use the group numbers of B and F to make an electron inventory, then allocate one electron from each partner to each single bond.

items.stem: Sketch a complete outer-shell dot-and-cross diagram of an isolated $\ce{PCl5}$ molecule, using dots from P and crosses from Cl. Include all lone pairs. State the total number of valence electrons and explain the electron count around P.

scheme.point: Five P–Cl single bonds, each one dot–cross shared pair.
Three cross–cross lone pairs on every Cl; none on P and no extra electrons.
Forty valence electrons overall: ten bonding and thirty in chlorine lone pairs.
Ten electrons surround P, so P has an expanded octet; the molecule has no overall charge.

items.explanation: The valence total is $5+5(7)=40$. Five shared pairs and fifteen chlorine lone pairs use all forty electrons; phosphorus is surrounded by ten bonding electrons and has no lone pair.
hints: Count the available outer-shell electrons before drawing any bonds.
Use one electron from each atom in an ordinary shared pair, then complete the terminal-atom shells.
Apply the same total-electron check even when the central atom is an octet-rule exception.

items.stem: Sketch a complete outer-shell dot-and-cross diagram of neutral $\ce{NO}$, using dots from N and crosses from O and an N=O double bond. Show all non-bonding electrons. State the total valence-electron count and explain why both atoms cannot have complete octets.

scheme.point: Two N–O shared dot–cross pairs represent the double bond.
One dot–dot lone pair and one unpaired dot on N; two cross–cross lone pairs on O.
Eleven electrons overall: four bonding, six in lone pairs and one unpaired; five dots and six crosses.
Seven electrons surround N and eight surround O. The neutral odd-electron molecule cannot give both atoms octets without changing its electron inventory.

items.explanation: NO supplies $5+6=11$ valence electrons. A double bond, one N lone pair, two O lone pairs and one unpaired N electron account for all eleven; adding an electron to complete the nitrogen octet would change the neutral species.
hints: An odd total cannot be divided entirely into pairs.
Track each atom’s original contribution as you distribute the non-bonding electrons.
Subtract the electrons already used by the stated double bond from each atom’s original outer-shell count.

flashcards.front: What does a dot-and-cross diagram show?
flashcards.back: Outer-shell electrons from different atoms, with shared and lone pairs and ionic charges where relevant.

flashcards.front: How is a coordinate bond represented?
flashcards.back: A shared pair whose two electrons were supplied by the same donor atom.

9701-3.7.1.motivate: A formula does not reveal where bonding electrons came from. Dot-and-cross diagrams let you account for every outer-shell electron and distinguish ionic, covalent and coordinate bonding.
9701-3.7.1.establish:
Use different symbols for electrons originally supplied by different atoms. For ionic bonding, show electron transfer, then draw separate ions in brackets with charges; for example, $\ce{MgO}$ contains $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$, with eight outer electrons on O. For covalent bonding, place one shared pair between atoms for each single bond, two for a double bond, and three for a triple bond; show remaining lone pairs. A coordinate bond is a shared pair whose two electrons came from one donor atom: the N lone pair of $\ce{NH3}$ is donated to $\ce{H+}$ when $\ce{NH4+}$ forms. Check the total valence-electron count, adjusting for ion charge. The octet rule has exceptions: B in $\ce{BF3}$ has six surrounding electrons, P in $\ce{PCl5}$ has ten, and an odd-electron species such as $\ce{NO}$ has an unpaired electron. Apply the same counting and origin rules to compounds from ionic bonding and molecular-shape topics, including $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ and $\ce{CO}$.
Foundation bridge: recall the neutral-atom valence counts from the periodic table and the meaning of ion charge. Read any stated bonding type or donor direction before choosing a structure; total electrons and local octets are different checks.
9701-3.7.1.connect: Ionic bonding transfers electrons before electrostatic attraction; covalent bonding shares pairs. A coordinate pair is still a covalent pair after it forms. The same electron-pair count helps predict molecular shapes.
9701-3.7.1.note:
- Ionic: separate bracketed ions with charges and transferred electrons.
- Covalent: shared pairs between atoms and any lone pairs.
- Coordinate: both electrons in the pair come from one donor.
- Check electron totals; allow incomplete octets, expanded octets and odd electrons.
- Count every electron once in the whole diagram; a shared pair counts around both bonded atoms when checking their shells.
9701-3.7.1.self_explain: How would your drawings of $\ce{MgO}$ and $\ce{NH4+}$ differ in brackets, charges and the origin of electron pairs?

discover.stem: In forming $\ce{NH4+}$ from $\ce{NH3}$ and $\ce{H+}$, where do the electrons in the new N–H pair originate?
discover.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair is donated to H⁺, which has no electron to contribute.

9701-3.7.1.plain_words: Start with the outer-shell electrons each atom supplies. Track their origins with two symbols: transfer them to form separate ions, or place pairs between atoms to show bonds. Count every electron once in the total, including lone pairs and any unpaired electron.

terms.meaning: Electrons in the outer shell, used to construct these bonding diagrams.
Two electrons between bonded atoms; both atoms count the pair towards their surrounding shell.
Two outer-shell electrons on one atom that are not shared in a bond.
A covalent bond in which one atom supplies both electrons of the shared pair.
Net charge after electron loss or gain; put it outside the bracket enclosing the ion.
terms.spoken: oxide ion with charge two minus

terms.meaning: More than eight electrons surrounding an atom in a bonding diagram.
A single electron that is not part of a bonding pair or lone pair.

forms.name: Ionic electron transfer
wordings: Sketch a dot-and-cross diagram for an ionic compound.
Show the transferred electrons, ion ratio, brackets and charges.
forms.example:
Worked example — ionic $\ce{MgO}$; use dots for O and crosses for Mg, omitting inner shells.
1. Count two outer electrons from Mg and six from O: eight to place. The 1:1 ratio allows Mg to transfer both electrons to O.
2. Draw separate $[\ce{Mg}]^{2+}$ and $[\ce{O}]^{2-}$ ions. Their charges sum to zero; the brackets enclose individual ions.
3. Put six dots and two crosses around O as four pairs. In this outer-shell transfer convention show no electrons on Mg and no shared pair between ions.
4. Check all eight original outer electrons are accounted for and the charges match the transfer.
forms.check: Sketch one formula unit of ionic $\ce{Mg2Si}$ using dots for original Si electrons and crosses for original Mg electrons. Draw every ion with its bracket and charge; omit inner shells and show no electrons on the Mg ions. Explain the electron transfer.
forms.answer: Two separate $[\ce{Mg}]^{2+}$ ions and one $[\ce{Si}]^{4-}$ ion. Si has four pairs containing four dots and four crosses in total. Each Mg supplies two crosses; there are no shared pairs between ions. Total charge $2(+2)-4=0$; eight original outer electrons are shown.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c3.7.pdf, pp.2–3; ER 9701 s19 P21 Q2 (bundle); original check and bookkeeping.

rubric.point: Two Mg ions and one Si ion, each separately bracketed, with charges 2+ on Mg and 4− on Si.
Si has eight outer electrons as four pairs: four original Si dots and four transferred Mg crosses.
Each Mg transfers two electrons; none are drawn on Mg and no shared pair joins the ions.

forms.name: Coordinate-pair origin and donor direction
wordings: Draw a dot-and-cross diagram showing the stated donor-to-acceptor direction.
Distinguish a coordinate shared pair from an ordinary shared pair.
forms.example:
Worked example — $\ce{CO}$, explicitly using the conventional oxygen-to-carbon donation requested by the question; dots for C, crosses for O.
1. Count $4+6=10$ valence electrons. Two ordinary C–O shared pairs use two dots and two crosses.
2. Add an O-supplied cross–cross shared pair: three shared pairs now lie between C and O.
3. The two remaining C dots form one lone pair on C; the two remaining O crosses form one lone pair on O.
4. Check four dots, six crosses and an octet around each atom. Label the donated pair $\ce{O -> C}$. CO is neutral overall; this diagram is an electron-origin convention.
forms.check: Water forms $\ce{H3O+}$ by donating an oxygen lone pair to $\ce{H+}$. Sketch its complete dot-and-cross diagram with dots from O and crosses from the two original H atoms. Label the donated pair and its donor-to-acceptor direction; include brackets and charge.
forms.answer: Three O–H shared pairs: two dot–cross pairs and one dot–dot pair donated from O to the incoming H; label $\ce{O -> H}$. One dot–dot lone pair remains on O. Enclose the whole ion in brackets with charge $+$. Six dots and two crosses give eight electrons; $\ce{H+}$ contributes none.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c3.7.pdf, p.6 (coordinate-pair rule); ER 9701 s22 P23 Q3 (CO direction, bundle); original hydronium check applying that rule.

rubric.point: Three O–H shared pairs: two ordinary dot–cross pairs and one oxygen-supplied dot–dot pair.
One oxygen lone pair remains; no additional electrons, giving eight electrons in total.
The donated pair goes from oxygen to the incoming hydrogen ion.
One bracket surrounds the whole hydronium ion, carrying one positive charge.

forms.name: Ordinary multiple bonds
wordings: Draw all shared pairs and lone pairs in a multiple-bonded molecule.
Check the total valence electrons and the electron count around each atom.
forms.example:
Worked example — $\ce{CO2}$, dots from C and crosses from either O.
1. Count $4+2(6)=16$ electrons and arrange O–C–O.
2. Put two dot–cross shared pairs in each C–O bond: two double bonds use eight electrons.
3. Each O retains two cross–cross lone pairs; C has no lone pair.
4. Count four dots and twelve crosses. All sixteen electrons are shown and each atom has an octet.
forms.check: Sketch a complete dot-and-cross diagram of $\ce{N2}$. Use dots from the left N and crosses from the right N. Include lone pairs and state the total valence-electron count.
forms.answer: Three dot–cross shared pairs form a triple bond. One dot–dot lone pair remains on the left N and one cross–cross lone pair on the right N. Ten valence electrons are shown, five from each atom, with eight surrounding each atom; no overall charge.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c3.7.pdf, pp.3–5; Cambridge 9701 syllabus 3.4.1 (multiple bonds) and 3.7.1; original example/check.

rubric.point: A triple bond represented by three shared dot–cross pairs.
One lone pair on each N, using dots on the left and crosses on the right, with no extra electrons.
Ten electrons overall, five originally from each N; eight surrounding each atom.

forms.name: Expanded-octet electron accounting
wordings: Draw a complete outer-shell diagram for an expanded-octet molecule.
Explain why an octet must not be forced on the central atom.
forms.example:
Worked example — an isolated $\ce{PCl5}$ molecule, dots from P and crosses from Cl.
1. Count $5+5(7)=40$ valence electrons.
2. Draw five P–Cl single bonds, each one dot–cross pair: ten bonding electrons.
3. Place three cross–cross lone pairs on each Cl: thirty more electrons. P has no lone pair.
4. All forty electrons are used. Each Cl has an octet, but the five shared pairs put ten electrons around P: an expanded octet. Do not add a central lone pair.
forms.check: Sketch the complete dot-and-cross diagram of $\ce{SF6}$ using dots from S and crosses from F. Show all lone pairs. State the total valence-electron count and the number surrounding S.
forms.answer: Six S–F single bonds, each one dot–cross shared pair; three cross–cross lone pairs on each F and none on S. There are $6+6(7)=48$ valence electrons overall: twelve bonding and thirty-six non-bonding. Twelve electrons surround S, an expanded octet; each F has eight.
forms.source: SaveMyExams/9701 a-level-chemistry-cie-25/9701 c3.7.pdf, pp.7–8; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf, p.22, 3.7.1; https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/7-3-lewis-symbols-and-structures (PCl5/SF6 Lewis structures).

rubric.point: Six S–F shared pairs, each containing one S dot and one F cross.
Three lone pairs on every F and no lone pair on S, with no extra electrons.
Forty-eight valence electrons in the whole molecule, of which twelve are bonding and thirty-six non-bonding.
Twelve electrons surround sulfur, so it has an expanded octet.

forms.name: Odd-electron species
wordings: Construct a diagram without inventing an electron to complete an octet.
Show lone pairs and an unpaired electron while conserving the total.
forms.example:
Worked example — neutral $\ce{NO}$; dots from N, crosses from O.
1. Count $5+6=11$ valence electrons. An odd total cannot be entirely paired.
2. Draw two ordinary dot–cross shared pairs, representing an N=O double bond.
3. Add one dot–dot lone pair and a single unpaired dot on N; put two cross–cross lone pairs on O.
4. Check five dots and six crosses. Four bonding electrons, six lone-pair electrons and one unpaired electron make eleven. O has eight surrounding electrons and N has seven; do not add an electron or a third bond.
forms.check: The neutral radical $\ce{NF2}$ has N bonded to two F atoms by single bonds. Sketch a dot-and-cross diagram with dots from N and crosses from F; show all remaining electrons. State the total valence electrons and the number surrounding N.
forms.answer: Two N–F dot–cross shared pairs; each F has three cross–cross lone pairs. N retains one dot–dot lone pair and one unpaired dot. Total $5+2(7)=19$ electrons: four bonding, fourteen in lone pairs and one unpaired. Seven electrons surround N; each F has eight. No ionic charge is added.
forms.source: https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664563-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf, p.22, 3.7.1; https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/7-3-lewis-symbols-and-structures (NO and the odd-electron method); original NF2 check with connectivity supplied.

rubric.point: Two N–F single bonds, each one dot–cross shared pair.
Three cross–cross lone pairs on each F; one dot–dot lone pair and one unpaired dot on N.
Nineteen electrons in total: four bonding, fourteen in lone pairs and one unpaired.
Seven electrons surround N, while each F has an octet; the radical is neutral.

guided_discover.stem: A dot electron and a cross electron are shown in the same diagram. Identify what the different symbols tell you.

options.A: The electrons have opposite electric charges.
options.B: The electrons originally came from different atoms.
options.C: Only the dot electron can form a bond.
options.D: The cross electron has a greater mass.

guided_discover.explanation: The symbols label original contributions. Both represent electrons with the same charge and mass; either can be in a bonding pair.

misconceptions.idea: Ionic formula units can be joined with ordinary shared pairs.
misconceptions.temptation: Treat the formula as a small covalent molecule.
misconceptions.fix: Follow the stated ionic model: transfer electrons, then draw separately bracketed ions in the required ratio with charges.

misconceptions.idea: The coordinate pair in the requested CO convention goes from C to O.
misconceptions.temptation: Choose an arrow from the written order of the atoms instead of the specified electron donor.
misconceptions.fix: Read the stated donor direction first. For this CO construction use two O symbols in the donated pair and label oxygen to carbon.

misconceptions.idea: Every atom must finish with exactly eight surrounding electrons.
misconceptions.temptation: Add an electron, remove a bond or hide an unpaired electron to force an octet.
misconceptions.fix: Conserve the electron inventory first; allow the expanded shell or unpaired electron required by the stated species.

misconceptions.idea: A coordinate shared pair must contain one electron from each atom.
misconceptions.temptation: Copy the symbols used for an ordinary covalent bond.
misconceptions.fix: Use two donor symbols for the coordinate pair, while still counting it as a shared bonding pair.
